\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can introduce myself in Arabic, give my name, and understand the other person's name.}

The whole introduction exchange, run once to a man and once to a woman: give a name, ask for one back, and close with tasharrafna.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{اسم}]{\ar{اسم} (ism) — \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-ism}



\begin{quote}
To introduce yourself you need \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{} — and it needs no new letters.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} All three are from Chapter 1: \textbf{\ar{ا}} (\emph{alif}), \textbf{\ar{س}} (\emph{sīn}), \textbf{\ar{م}} (\emph{mīm}). Read \textbf{\ar{اسم}} right to left $\to$ \textbf{ism}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{اسم}} (\emph{ism}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}), root \textbf{s–m–w}. It is a \textbf{Semitic} word, cousin of Hebrew \emph{shem} (\textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) — the same pairing you saw with \emph{salām} / \emph{shalom}. It has \emph{no} tie to the Indo-European \emph{name} / Latin \emph{nōmen}: Arabic is a different family entirely, and its word for \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{} is its own.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read right to left — \textquotedblleft{}ism\textquotedblright{}
  \item its Hebrew cousin — \emph{shem}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What family does \textbf{\ar{اسم}} belong to, and what Hebrew word is its cousin? (Semitic; \emph{shem}. Not related to English \emph{name}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{ي}]{\ar{ي} (-ī) — \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} a letter stuck on the end}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-ii-my}



\begin{quote}
Arabic has no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} — it glues one letter onto the noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} \textbf{\ar{ي}} (\emph{yāʾ}), met in \emph{ʿalaykum} — here it does a new job: attached to the end of a noun, it means \textquotedblleft{}my.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
Arabic builds \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} by \textbf{suffix}, not a separate word: \textbf{\ar{اسم}} (\emph{ism}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ar{ي}} (\emph{-ī}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) = \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} (\emph{ismī}, \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{}). This is the same trick as the attached \textbf{al-} (\textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}) from Chapter 1 — Arabic loves to fasten little pieces onto a word rather than string separate words together.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ism\textquotedblright{} + \textquotedblleft{}-ī\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}ismī\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{})
  \item the pattern — Arabic glues \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} on, like it glued \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} (\emph{al-})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Arabic say \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} and what is \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{}? (A suffix \textbf{\ar{ي}} (-ī) glued on; \emph{ismī}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{اسمي} …]{\ar{اسمي} … (ismī …) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…,\textquotedblright{} with no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-ismii}



\begin{quote}
Assemble it — and notice the missing word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The phrase, assembled}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ism (name) + -ī (my) + your name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{اسمي} …} = \textquotedblleft{}my-name …\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ismī Arun.} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — again}]
Recall from \emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} (Ch. 1) that Arabic sets two words side by side and lets \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} be understood. So \emph{ismī Arun} is literally \textquotedblleft{}my-name Arun.\textquotedblright{} Arabic shares this \textbf{zero copula} with the Dravidian languages (Tamil \emph{eṉ peyar Arun}) — two unrelated families meeting on the same habit.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ismī …\textquotedblright{} with your name
  \item notice — no word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name in Arabic. (\emph{Ismī ….}) What does Arabic leave out, and which other family does the same? (The verb \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — the zero copula, shared with the Dravidian languages.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{أنت}]{\ar{أنت} (anta / anti) — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} marked by \emph{gender}}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-anta-anti}



\begin{quote}
To ask a name you need \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — and Arabic's is unlike any you've met: it changes with the \emph{listener's} gender.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} Two new letters: \textbf{\ar{أ}} (\emph{alif} with a \emph{hamza} seat, a glottal \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}-start) and \textbf{\ar{ت}} (\emph{tāʾ}, \textquotedblleft{}t\textquotedblright{} — the \ar{ب}/\ar{ت}/\ar{ث} skeleton from Ch. 1, two dots above). The final vowel is a mark: \textbf{\ar{أنتَ}} \emph{anta}, \textbf{\ar{أنتِ}} \emph{anti}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أنت}} is \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — but Arabic splits it by the listener's \textbf{gender}: \textbf{anta} to a man, \textbf{anti} to a woman. (Note the Semitic \emph{-ta}/\emph{-ti} ending — the same \emph{t} that marks \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} in Hebrew \emph{atta}/\emph{att}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a different axis of \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}}]
The European and Dravidian tracks split \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} by \textbf{register} (familiar vs. respectful — \emph{tū/vous}, \emph{nī/nīṅgaḷ}). Arabic splits it by \textbf{gender}: \emph{anta} (to a man) vs. \emph{anti} (to a woman). Same pronoun, a wholly different distinction — you choose by \emph{who you're talking to}, not how formal you are.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}anta\textquotedblright{} (to a man), \textquotedblleft{}anti\textquotedblright{} (to a woman)
  \item the contrast — European/Dravidian split by register, Arabic by gender
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Arabic split \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} and how is that different from French or Tamil? (By \textbf{gender} — \emph{anta} (m.) / \emph{anti} (f.); the others split by register.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{ما}]{\ar{ما} (mā) — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-maa}



\begin{quote}
The question-word — and you already read it as a warm-up in Chapter 1.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} No new letters: \textbf{\ar{م}} (\emph{m}) + \textbf{\ar{ا}} (\emph{alif}, long \emph{ā}) $\to$ \textbf{\ar{ما}} \emph{mā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{ما}} (\emph{mā}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) is the everyday question-word for things. (Arabic has a second, \emph{māḏā}, for \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} before verbs; \emph{mā} is the one you want before a noun, as in \textquotedblleft{}what {[}is{]} your name?\textquotedblright{})
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mā\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mā ismuka?\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}what {[}is{]} your name?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{ما}} mean, and when is it used? (\textquotedblleft{}What,\textquotedblright{} before a noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟}]{\ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟} (mā ismuka / ismuki) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-maa-ismuka}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the question — what + your-name — no \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} gender in the suffix.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The phrase, assembled}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{اسمك}} = \textbf{\ar{اسم}} (\emph{ism}, name) + \textbf{\ar{ك}} (\emph{kāf}, the \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{} suffix) — and it too is \textbf{gendered}: \emph{ismuka} (a man's name), \emph{ismuki} (a woman's).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟}} = literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{what {[}is{]} your-name?}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

No \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} the possessive glued on, the gender carried in the suffix.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the matched suffixes}]
\textquotedblleft{}My name\textquotedblright{} takes \textbf{\ar{ي}} (\emph{-ī}), \textquotedblleft{}your name\textquotedblright{} takes \textbf{\ar{ك}} (\emph{-ka/-ki}). The suffixes \emph{are} the grammar of the exchange. Answer with \emph{ismī Arun}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mā ismuka?\textquotedblright{} (to a man), \textquotedblleft{}mā ismuki?\textquotedblright{} (to a woman)
  \item ask, then answer — \textquotedblleft{}mā ismuka?\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}ismī …\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟}} literally say, and where is the gender marked? (\textquotedblleft{}What your-name?\textquotedblright{}; in the suffix — \emph{-ka} (m.) / \emph{-ki} (f.).)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{تشرفنا}]{\ar{تشرفنا} (tasharrafnā) — \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-tasharrafna}



\begin{quote}
The warm close — and it presents the meeting as an honour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Arabic.)} Uses \textbf{\ar{ت}} (\emph{tāʾ}, just met), \textbf{\ar{ش}} (\emph{shīn}) and \textbf{\ar{ر}} (\emph{rāʾ}) from Ch. 1, plus \textbf{\ar{ف}} (\emph{fāʾ}, \textquotedblleft{}f\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{تشرفنا}} (\emph{tasharrafnā}), root \textbf{sh–r–f} (\emph{honour, nobility}): \emph{sharaf} (\textquotedblleft{}honour\textquotedblright{}), \emph{sharīf} (\textquotedblleft{}noble\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{Sharif} of Mecca, and distantly the title behind English \emph{sheriff}). \emph{tasharrafnā} means literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we have been honoured}\textquotedblright{} — to meet you is presented as an honour received. A more literal option is \textbf{\ar{فرصة} \ar{سعيدة}} (\emph{furṣa saʿīda}, \textquotedblleft{}a happy occasion\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tasharrafnā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root family — \emph{sharaf} (honour), \emph{sharīf} (noble)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{تشرفنا}} literally mean, and from what root? (\textquotedblleft{}We have been honoured\textquotedblright{}; \emph{sh–r–f}, \textquotedblleft{}honour.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — the introduction, whole}

\label{lesson:AR-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
You could already greet someone. Every lesson since has been building one short exchange: give your name, ask for theirs, close warmly. Here it is whole.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Read right to left:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\ar{اسمي} \ar{ميرا}. (\emph{ismī Mira}) & My name is Mira. \\
\ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟} (\emph{mā ismuka}) & What's your name? \\
\ar{اسمي} \ar{أرون}. (\emph{ismī Arun}) & My name is Arun. \\
\ar{تشرفنا}. (\emph{tasharrafnā}) & Pleased to meet you. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the pieces}
Every piece from the root-and-suffix engine:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ism} $\leftarrow$ root \emph{s–m–w} (Hebrew \emph{shem}, \emph{not} English \emph{name})
  \item the glued \textbf{-ī} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{-ka/-ki} (\textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{tasharrafnā} $\leftarrow$ root \emph{sh–r–f} (\textquotedblleft{}honour\textquotedblright{}; \emph{sharīf}, \emph{sheriff})
\end{itemize}

Two Arabic habits: it drops \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} entirely (the \textbf{zero copula}, shared with the Dravidian languages), and it marks \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} by \textbf{gender} (\emph{anta}/\emph{anti}), not register.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, right to left
  \item your own introduction — \textquotedblleft{}ismī …, tasharrafnā\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask it back — \textquotedblleft{}mā ismuka?\textquotedblright{} (to a man) / \textquotedblleft{}mā ismuki?\textquotedblright{} (to a woman)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name, ask someone else's, say you're pleased. (\emph{Ismī …. / Mā ismuka? / Tasharrafnā.}) Two things Arabic does differently from the European tracks? (No word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — zero copula; and \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} split by \emph{gender}, not register.)

Next chapter: \emph{kayfa ḥāluka?} (\textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{al-ḥamdu lillāh} — the responding cycle.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nūn, tāʾ, thāʾ]{\ar{ن،} \ar{ت،} \ar{ث} — one bowl, four dot-patterns}

\label{lesson:AR-W04-dots-family-nun-ta}



\begin{quote}
In Lesson 3 you drew \textbf{\ar{ب}} (\emph{bāʾ}) — a boat-bowl with \textbf{one dot below} — and met the idea that the \textbf{dots make the letter}. Now the promised payoff: the \emph{same} bowl, with the dots moved and multiplied, gives you three more common letters. Learn the bowl once; the dots do the rest.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — The bowl family — a truth-table}
Every letter here is the \textbf{same shallow boat-bowl} you already draw for \emph{bāʾ}. Only the dots change:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{the dots} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{ب}} \emph{bāʾ} & b & one dot \textbf{below} (from Lesson 3) \\
\textbf{\ar{ن}} \emph{nūn} & n & one dot \textbf{above} \\
\textbf{\ar{ت}} \emph{tāʾ} & t & \textbf{two} dots above \\
\textbf{\ar{ث}} \emph{thāʾ} & th & \textbf{three} dots above \\
(\ar{ح} \emph{ḥāʾ}) & ḥ & \textbf{no} dot (a bigger hook — Lesson 3's cousin) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read it as a dial: \textbf{below $\to$ 1 above $\to$ 2 above $\to$ 3 above}. The pen-stroke is identical each time; your only real decision is \emph{how many dots, and on which side}.

\subsection*{Script — Draw them}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ن}} (\emph{nūn}) — the bowl, then \textbf{one dot above}. (\emph{nūn} sits a little deeper than \emph{bāʾ} when it stands alone, but joined, it is the shared skeleton + one dot.) From Phoenician \textbf{nun}, \textquotedblleft{}fish\textquotedblright{} — ancestor of Greek \emph{nu} and Latin \textbf{N}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ت}} (\emph{tāʾ}) — the bowl, then \textbf{two dots above}. From Phoenician \textbf{taw}, \textquotedblleft{}mark\textquotedblright{} — the great-grandparent of Latin \textbf{T} (and the word \emph{tattoo}-like \textquotedblleft{}mark\textquotedblright{} survives in \emph{taw} meaning a cross-mark).
  \item \textbf{\ar{ث}} (\emph{thāʾ}) — the bowl, then \textbf{three dots above} (drawn as a little triangle of dots).
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — Where you have seen them — \ar{أنت}}
The Chapter 2 word \textbf{\ar{أنت}} (\emph{anta / anti}, \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) is built from exactly these: an \emph{alif} (with a small \textbf{hamza} seat you will meet in Lesson 6), then \textbf{\ar{ن}} (\emph{nūn}, one dot above) joined to \textbf{\ar{ت}} (\emph{tāʾ}, two dots above). So \emph{\ar{أنت}} is, in dots, \textquotedblleft{}bowl-with-one-above, bowl-with-two-above\textquotedblright{} — you can now read the skeleton of a real word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} the same bowl four times, then dot them — \ar{ب} (1 below), \ar{ن} (1 above), \ar{ت} (2 above), \ar{ث} (3 above)
  \item \emph{Say it:} the dial — \textquotedblleft{}below, one above, two above, three above — b, n, t, th\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Write it:} the joined pair \textbf{\ar{نت}} (\emph{nūn}$\to$\emph{tāʾ}), the core of \emph{\ar{أنت}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What single feature separates \textbf{\ar{ب}, \ar{ن}, \ar{ت}, \ar{ث}}? (\textbf{The dots} — same bowl; one below / one above / two above / three above.) Which two of them build the Chapter 2 word \textbf{\ar{أنت}} (\textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{})? (\textbf{\ar{ن}} \emph{nūn} and \textbf{\ar{ت}} \emph{tāʾ}.) What Latin letters descend from \emph{nūn} and \emph{taw}? (\textbf{N} and \textbf{T}.) Next: \textbf{\ar{ي}} (\emph{yāʾ}), the two-dots-below letter — and your name.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yāʾ]{\ar{ي} (yāʾ) — the last dot-letter, and \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-W05-ya-and-my-name}



\begin{quote}
One more member of the bowl family, and it is a \textbf{triple threat}: \textbf{\ar{ي}} (\emph{yāʾ}) is a consonant \emph{y}, \textbf{and} the long vowel \textbf{ī}, \textbf{and} the little suffix \textbf{-ī} meaning \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{my}.\textquotedblright{} With it you can finally write a whole Chapter 2 phrase in your own hand: \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} (\textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{}).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — \ar{ي} (yāʾ) — two dots below}
Break it apart:

1. \textbf{the body} — the boat-bowl (standing alone) or a tooth (when joined). 2. \textbf{two dots BELOW} — the mark that completes the bowl-family dial: \emph{bāʾ} had one below, \emph{yāʾ} has \textbf{two} below.

So the full \textquotedblleft{}below/above\textquotedblright{} set is now closed: \textbf{\ar{ب}} one-below, \textbf{\ar{ي}} two-below; \textbf{\ar{ن}} one-above, \textbf{\ar{ت}} two-above, \textbf{\ar{ث}} three-above. \emph{Yāʾ} comes from Phoenician \textbf{yod}, \textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{} — the ancestor of Greek \emph{iota} and Latin \textbf{I / J} (and the reason we say \textquotedblleft{}not one \textbf{iota},\textquotedblright{} the smallest letter).

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Its three jobs}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{consonant y} — as in \emph{yawm} (\textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{long vowel ī} — a \emph{seat} for the \textquotedblleft{}ee\textquotedblright{} sound.
  \item \textbf{the suffix \ar{ـي} \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}} — the Chapter 2 possessive. Glue \emph{-ī} onto a noun and it becomes \textquotedblleft{}my \_\_\_,\textquotedblright{} exactly as \emph{ism} (\textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-ī} $\to$ \emph{ismī} (\textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — Assemble — first \ar{اسم}, then \ar{اسمي}}
You already know every letter of \textbf{\ar{اسم}} (\emph{ism}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) from Lessons 1–3: \textbf{\ar{ا}} (alif) · \textbf{\ar{س}} (sīn) · \textbf{\ar{م}} (mīm). Write it right-to-left:

1. \textbf{\ar{ا}} (\emph{alif}) — the upright; it \textbf{does not join} forward, so the pen lifts. 2. \textbf{\ar{س}} (\emph{sīn}) — three teeth, joining into… 3. \textbf{\ar{م}} (\emph{mīm}) — round head + tail. $\to$ \textbf{\ar{اسم}}.

Now add \textbf{\ar{ي}} for \textquotedblleft{}my.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Mīm} joins forward to \emph{yāʾ}, giving \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} (\emph{ismī}):

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} = \emph{alif · sīn · mīm · yāʾ} = \emph{i-s-m-ī} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{my name}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Read it back, right to left, and you have written a phrase you will say every time you introduce yourself.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ar{ي}} — body + \textbf{two dots below}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the closed dial — \textquotedblleft{}\ar{ب} one-below, \ar{ي} two-below; \ar{ن}/\ar{ت}/\ar{ث} one/two/three above\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ar{اسم}} (ism), then extend to \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} (ismī, \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where do \emph{yāʾ}'s dots sit, and how many? (\textbf{Two, below.}) Name \emph{yāʾ}'s \textbf{three} jobs. (Consonant \emph{y}; long vowel \emph{ī}; the suffix \emph{-ī} \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{my}.\textquotedblright{}) Spell \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} letter by letter, right to left. (\emph{alif · sīn · mīm · yāʾ} — \textquotedblleft{}my name.\textquotedblright{}) Next: the little \textbf{vowel marks} — and how one of them flips \emph{\ar{أنت}} from \textquotedblleft{}you (m.)\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}you (f.).\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fatḥa, kasra, ḍamma; hamza]{\ar{َ} \ar{ِ} \ar{ُ} — the short vowels the abjad usually hides}

\label{lesson:AR-W06-harakat-and-hamza}



\begin{quote}
In the first writing cluster you learned Arabic is an \textbf{abjad}: short vowels are \textbf{usually left out}. This lesson shows the marks that a beginner's book \emph{does} print when it wants to be clear—the \textbf{ḥarakāt}—and one of them delivers the neatest payoff in the whole set: the difference between \textquotedblleft{}you (m.)\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}you (f.)\textquotedblright{} is a \textbf{single dash}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — The ḥarakāt — three short-vowel marks}
These are small marks written \textbf{around} a consonant, not letters in their own right. On the letter \emph{bāʾ} (\textbf{\ar{ب}}):

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{name} & \textbf{where} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{َ}} & \emph{fatḥa} & a slash \textbf{above} & \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{\ar{بَ}} = \emph{ba} \\
\textbf{\ar{ِ}} & \emph{kasra} & a slash \textbf{below} & \textquotedblleft{}i\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{\ar{بِ}} = \emph{bi} \\
\textbf{\ar{ُ}} & \emph{ḍamma} & a tiny \emph{wāw} \textbf{above} & \textquotedblleft{}u\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{\ar{بُ}} = \emph{bu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Stop at these three vowel marks. The next four-minute micro-lesson adds the separate ideas “no vowel,” “double this consonant,” and the \emph{-an} ending. Their shapes wait there so this page never asks you to absorb two writing steps at once.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The payoff — \ar{أنتَ} vs \ar{أنتِ}}
Here is why the marks matter. The Chapter 2 word \textbf{\ar{أنت}} (\textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) is the \emph{same} consonant skeleton for a man and a woman — \emph{alif · nūn · tāʾ}. What splits them is a single ḥaraka on the final \textbf{\ar{ت}}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أنتَ}} — \emph{tāʾ} + \textbf{fatḥa} (the \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} slash above) = \textbf{anta}, \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to a \textbf{man}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{أنتِ}} — \emph{tāʾ} + \textbf{kasra} (the \textquotedblleft{}i\textquotedblright{} slash below) = \textbf{anti}, \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to a \textbf{woman}.
\end{itemize}

One dash up or down carries the whole gender distinction you learned in the introductions chapter. Leave the mark off — as normal Arabic does — and \textbf{\ar{أنت}} serves both, the reader deciding from context.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} on \textbf{\ar{ب}} — \emph{fatḥa} above (\emph{ba}), \emph{kasra} below (\emph{bi}), \emph{ḍamma} above (\emph{bu})
  \item \emph{Say it:} the flip — \textquotedblleft{}\ar{أنتَ} \emph{anta} (man, slash above) vs \ar{أنتِ} \emph{anti} (woman, slash below)\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the \textbf{ḥarakāt}, and does everyday text show them? (The short- \textbf{vowel marks} — \emph{fatḥa/kasra/ḍamma}; normally \textbf{left off}, since Arabic is an abjad.) Which mark, and where, turns \emph{anta} into \emph{anti}? (A \emph{kasra} — the \textquotedblleft{}i\textquotedblright{} slash—\textbf{below} the final \emph{tāʾ}, instead of the \emph{fatḥa} above.) You have now made one consonant skeleton say \emph{anta} or \emph{anti} with one tiny mark.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sukūn, shadda, fatḥatan]{\ar{ْ} \ar{ّ} \ar{ً} — stop, double, or add \emph{-an}}

\label{lesson:AR-W06-sukun-shadda-tanwin}



\begin{quote}
You already know the three short-vowel marks. Keep those shapes in mind. This lesson adds exactly three more marks, one job at a time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — Three marks, three instructions}
Each mark sits around a consonant. It changes how you read that consonant; it is not another full letter.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{name} & \textbf{instruction} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{ْ}} & \emph{sukūn} & stop: no vowel follows this consonant \\
\textbf{\ar{ّ}} & \emph{shadda} & hold or double this consonant \\
\textbf{\ar{ً}} & \emph{fatḥatan} & add the ending \emph{-an} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look at the last mark in \textbf{\ar{شكرًا}} (\emph{shukran}, “thank you”). The small doubled stroke above the final letter supplies \emph{-an}. You have seen the word before; today you are learning what that one mark tells the reader.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} draw \textbf{\ar{ْ}} once — a small circle above the line; say “no vowel”
  \item \emph{Write it:} draw \textbf{\ar{ّ}} once — a small \emph{w} above the line; say “double”
  \item \emph{Write it:} draw \textbf{\ar{ً}} once — two light slashes above the line; say “-an”
  \item \emph{Say it:} point in order — \emph{sukūn}, \emph{shadda}, \emph{fatḥatan}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which mark means “no vowel”? (\textbf{\ar{ْ}}, \emph{sukūn}.) Which doubles a consonant? (\textbf{\ar{ّ}}, \emph{shadda}.) Which gives \emph{shukran} its \emph{-an} ending? (\textbf{\ar{ً}}, \emph{fatḥatan}.) Trace each once more without rushing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hamza]{\ar{ء} and \ar{أ} — the glottal catch}

\label{lesson:AR-W06-hamza}



\begin{quote}
The marks in the last lesson supplied vowels. \textbf{Hamza} is different: it writes a real consonant sound.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — The catch in “uh-oh”}
Say English “uh-oh” slowly. The little catch between the two syllables is a \textbf{glottal stop}. Arabic writes that consonant with \textbf{\ar{ء}}, called \textbf{hamza}.

Hamza often sits on a \textbf{seat}. At the start of \textbf{\ar{أنت}} (\emph{anta/anti}, “you”), it rides above \textbf{\ar{ا}}, producing \textbf{\ar{أ}}. The \emph{alif} supplies the seat; the hamza marks the glottal-stop consonant.

That gives \emph{alif} two roles you must keep separate:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ا}} can carry long \emph{ā}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{أ}} can be an \emph{alif} seat bearing the consonant \textbf{\ar{ء}}.
\end{itemize}

Hamza is therefore not another short-vowel mark. Its sound is the catch itself.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “uh-oh” and feel the glottal catch
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ar{ء}} alone, then \textbf{\ar{أ}} on its \emph{alif} seat
  \item \emph{Point to:} \textbf{\ar{أنتَ} / \ar{أنتِ}} — the same initial hamza in both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is hamza a vowel mark? (\textbf{No.}) What sound does it write? (\textbf{A glottal stop.}) What is \textbf{\ar{أ}}? (\textbf{Hamza riding on an alif seat.})
\end{tcolorbox}
